blocks.heading: What this section covers
blocks.text: Analyse form, structure and language and how they work together; show how several choices combine to create one meaning or effect; write about effects precisely.

blocks.heading: The three grounds
blocks.text: Form covers the kind of text and its conventions; structure covers the organisation of the whole text — its opening, sequence, shifts of focus, paragraphing and ending; language covers the choices inside sentences: words, images, grammar, sound. The three are grounds, not headings: an analysis need not take them in separate sections, and a point that joins a structural choice to a language choice is usually the stronger for it.

blocks.heading: Structure is a system of decisions
blocks.text: The structural features worth analysing in a non-fiction text are its opening and what it promises, its shifts of focus, its paragraph lengths, its sequence, its repetition across the text, and its ending. Each is a place a writer made a decision — what to tell first, where to turn, how long to stay, what to echo, how to leave — and the analysis names the decision and its effect, never just the location.

blocks.heading: Effect
blocks.text: An effect is what a writer’s choice leads the reader to think, feel or do at that point in the text, and it is not the same as what the words mean: "the water arrives sideways" means fog, and its effect is to surprise the reader into reading on. The analytical sequence runs feature, evidence, effect on this reader, link to the text’s purpose — four moves, in that order, until they are habit.

blocks.heading: Choices that work together
blocks.text: Several choices can work together towards one effect, so the strongest analysis shows how a structural choice and a language choice support each other: a text that opens and closes in the same place, and uses the same image at both, makes its ending an arrival rather than a stop. Analysing features as a system means tracing that joint effect rather than listing devices one by one — the text’s meaning is made by combinations, and the paragraph that shows a combination says something no list can.

blocks.heading: Worked example: two choices, one effect
blocks.text: From a feature on a night rescue: the structural choice is a single one-sentence paragraph — "By midnight, the boy was out." — and the language choice inside it is the passive, which names no rescuer. Together they make the rescue feel like the mountain’s decision rather than any person’s achievement, and the analysis that shows the pairing has argued something about the text: that it credits the place, not the team. One effect, two choices, one point — which is the shape of the strongest paragraphs.

blocks.heading: Worked example: one choice, all four moves
blocks.text: Take this sentence from an appeal leaflet, written for the purpose: "Your N$150 is a bookcase’s twelfth shelf." The feature is the concrete arithmetic — a donation translated into a piece of furniture. The evidence is the exact words, quoted. The effect: the reader is made to picture their own money standing inside a classroom, which turns a transfer into a placement, and the reader who can see the twelfth shelf has already agreed to its existence. The link to purpose: the leaflet exists to convert generosity into specifics, and this sentence converts N$150 into wood — the four moves, in one sentence of analysis, and the sequence done is the sequence learned.

blocks.heading: Form and structure held together
blocks.text: A charity appeal opens with the problem, moves to the mechanism, prices the gift, and closes on the children. That is structure. The same appeal is a leaflet — headings, direct address, a call to action — and that is form. A strong point names both and shows them working together: the leaflet’s heading convention ("Give a classroom a bookcase") promises the structure’s first move, so the form opens the door the structure walks through. An analysis that treats form as a list at the start and structure as a route in the middle has described a filing system; an analysis that shows them shaking hands has analysed a text. And the language sits inside both, which is why the strongest points are often the hardest to file: a leaflet’s imperative verbs are language, but their placing in the closing paragraph is structure, and the analysis that says the imperative arrives last, when the reader has been made ready to act, has joined all three grounds in one sentence. The task names form, structure and language as the ground it rewards; it does not name them as three separate rooms. The analysis that treats them as one working machine is describing what the writer actually built.

blocks.heading: The four moves on a hard case
blocks.text: Some choices resist the sequence, and the resistance is instructive. A single word’s connotation is easy to run: feature (the noun), evidence ("rumour"), effect (rain made half-believed), link (the piece’s purpose of making the reader feel the dryness). A structural choice is harder, because its evidence is a place rather than a phrase: the feature is the held-back rescue, the evidence is "the account of the rescue is held back until the final paragraph" with the reader directed to the arrangement, the effect is the reader spending the piece asking whether it succeeded, and the link is the suspense the piece exists to build. Run the sequence on the hard cases too, and let the evidence bend to the choice — the sequence is the same, and only the quotation changes shape.

blocks.heading: Summary and spot-naming
blocks.text: Two errors hollow an analysis out. Retelling or summarising the text, often at length, replaces analysis with content, and the cure is the anchor rule: content is mentioned only to anchor a point about a choice. Naming devices and sentence types without saying what any of them does is feature-spotting, and it earns little; the deletion test catches it — remove the device’s name from the sentence, and if nothing about meaning or effect is left, nothing was analysed.
